To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

academics have a range of different drivers and motivations, including the need to produce knowledge that is useful and relevant to the world outside academia, that academics are constrained by their career biographies and the disciplinary background they come from and that academics are also subject to contradictory pressures from their institutions.

the barriers to knowledge exchange in the UK are not only about the different drivers and practices of academics and policymakers, but also about the institutional and career pressures that academics face.

academics are motivated by different drivers than policymakers and civil servants, and that this can lead to misunderstandings about the nature of research, and the way it is conducted and communicated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the ways in which academics make sense of the knowledge exchange process and what this means for policymakers.
the everyday practices of academics and how they make sense of what they are doing.
the question of what academics are doing in the contemporary university and the ways in evidence is being produced in the university.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the co-production of this research has enabled us to identify the ways that the contemporary academic environment can be both a barrier and an enabler of knowledge exchange.
academics and civil servants need to work together more collaboratively and that the academic community needs to be more reflective on their own practices.
academics and policymakers have different ways of working and that these differences can be overcome if both sides understand the different ways of working.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
academics are often not aware of what policymakers need and policymakers are not aware of what academics do and the pressures on them.
we need to develop a new understanding of what we mean by knowledge exchange, and how we can develop more collaborative approaches that can help to overcome the barriers that exist.
the more that policymakers and civil servants can understand how academics think about their own work, the more likely it is that the evidence they produce will be used.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the barriers to knowledge exchange are more to do with the way in which the university is currently organised than with the individual academics.
the barriers to knowledge exchange are complex, and that there is no ‘magic bullet’ solution.
there needs to be a more nuanced understanding of the ways in which academics work, which can only be achieved by working together.
